Acmerun provides managed fine-tuning: you choose an open base model and a training recipe for a dataset, and the run is managed for you, with live progress and the trained weights when it succeeds. Acmerun uses a prepaid wallet. You add credit to your account and usage is deducted per second while a rented GPU works on your run (from fetching the dataset to uploading the weights) and while a deployment's replica is up. Every run (machine launch) costs at least €1 ($1.15): if its per-second charge comes to less, €1 is charged instead; the quote before you start shows it. Unused credit does not expire while your account is open.

You pay in US dollars or euros, whichever you choose. The balance is kept in US dollars and shown in your currency; a euro top-up is credited at the rate shown when you pay. A whole run is charged once — a single entry in your billing ledger covering the run's total metered cost — when the run reaches a finished state.
A run starts only when its dataset passed our checks and your balance covers the run's estimate, both before anything is charged.
If your balance reaches zero, a running job is automatically stopped and the partial cost is logged in your ledger, to prevent negative balances.

Host failure. If the GPU machine training your run dies or stops answering, we start the run again on a new machine once, and the time used on the failed machine is refunded. If the run still cannot finish, or fails for any other reason on our side, the whole run is refunded to your balance.
A completed run's weights stay in our private storage, at no charge, until you delete them. There is no storage fee, no account fee and no processing fee.

GPU time is charged per second while a replica is up, plus a routing fee per request, at the rates on the pricing page. __Host-next-auth.csrf-token (cookie): protects form submissions against cross-site request forgery. It is set on your first visit, before you sign in and whether or not you ever do.

Loss is the single number Acmerun's run monitor updates most often, and it's the best signal for whether a fine-tune is working.

A healthy run shows a steep early descent as the model adapts to your dataset's format, followed by a slower, steadier decline as it refines. A curve that plateaus early, or barely moves, usually points to a learning-rate or dataset-size issue rather than a recipe problem.

Because Acmerun's run report keeps the final loss alongside your dataset name, recipe, and cost, it's easy to compare across runs when you're iterating on the same dataset with different recipes or base models.

LoRA vs QLoRA vs full fine-tune: which recipe should you pick?
LoRA — Fast freezes the base model and trains small low-rank adapter matrices on top of it. It's the cheapest and quickest recipe, and a great first run for style or tone adaptation.
lines.section: LoRA vs QLoRA vs full fine-tune: which recipe should you pick?

lines.text: QLoRA — Balanced quantizes the base model to 4-bit precision before applying LoRA adapters, which means you can fine-tune larger models on a smaller GPU tier at a modest quality tradeoff.
lines.section: LoRA vs QLoRA vs full fine-tune: which recipe should you pick?

lines.text: Full fine-tune — Max updates every weight in the model. It's the slowest and most expensive recipe, and it's the one to reach for once you've validated an approach with LoRA and need to push quality further.
lines.section: LoRA vs QLoRA vs full fine-tune: which recipe should you pick?

lines.text: A reasonable default: start with LoRA — Fast to validate your dataset and prompt format, then move to QLoRA or a full fine-tune once you know the run is worth scaling up.
